title: After the Victory
subtitle: The Humaneness of Prisoners, the Ransom of Literacy, and the Shock in Makkah
summary: The dignified burial of the fallen, the Prophet addressing the fallen chieftains in the well of Badr, unprecedented humane treatment of seventy prisoners of war, the consultation on ransom, teaching literacy to Madinan children as a path to freedom, and the grief and vows of revenge in Makkah.

sections.text: Fourteen Muslims were killed, six of the Muhajirun and eight of the Ansar, in the count the sirah usually gives. Abu Talha, in Sahih al-Bukhari 3976, as Anas reported it from him, says the Prophet ordered that twenty-four leaders of Quraysh be thrown into a dry, foul well of Badr. The hadith does not give a motive of sanitation.

On the third day he halted at the lip of the well and called them by their names and their fathers' names. The wording Bukhari preserves is: 'O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, and O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, would it have pleased you to have obeyed God and His Messenger? We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?' Umar said, 'O Messenger of God, you are speaking to bodies that have no souls.' He replied, 'By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you do not hear what I say better than they do.' The narrator Qatada added that God gave them hearing so that they might be rebuked. That sentence is Qatada's, not the Prophet's. The report is Abu Talha's, not Ibn Umar's, and it is not Bukhari 4043, which belongs to Uhud.
The quiet desert reaches where ethical standards of warfare were first established.

The Muslims marched back to Madinah escorting seventy prisoners of war, representing the elite of Makkah. In ancient warfare, captives were routinely tortured, mutilated, or sold into brutal slavery. The Prophet, however, issued an unambiguous command to his companions: 'I enjoin you to treat the prisoners with kindness' (Istawsu bi al-asara khayra).

The companions implemented this command with astonishing devotion. Abu Aziz ibn Umayr, brother of Mus'ab, later recounted: 'I was among the captives of Badr. Whenever the Muslims sat down to eat morning or evening meals, they would give me the bread while they ate only dates, out of obedience to the Messenger of God's injunction! Whenever a piece of bread fell into the hand of one of them, he would immediately hand it to me.'
Consultation on Ransom and the Price of Literacy

Muslim 1763, still Umar's report, says the Prophet asked Abu Bakr and Umar what they thought of the captives. Abu Bakr said they were kin, and that a ransom would be a strength, and that God might guide them. Umar said he did not hold that view: they should be killed, and he named Aqil for Ali and a relative of his own. The Prophet inclined to Abu Bakr and not to Umar.

The next day Umar found the Prophet and Abu Bakr in tears. The Prophet said he wept because of what had been shown him of a punishment for his companions, close as a nearby tree, on account of their taking the ransom. The sums of one thousand to four thousand dirhams, and the condition that a captive who could write might teach ten children of Madinah, are the sirah, not this hadith. Later writers name Zayd ibn Thabit among the children taught that way. That, too, is sirah.

مَا كَانَ لِنَبِيٍّ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُ أَسْرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ يُثْخِنَ فِي الْأَرْضِ ۚ تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ الدُّنْيَا وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ الْآخِرَةَ ۗ وَاللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ
'It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has thoroughly subdued in the land. You desire the goods of this world, while God desires the Hereafter. And God is Exalted in Might, Wise.' (Surah al-Anfal 8:67)

Muslim 1763 joins this verse to that morning. The next verse, 8:68, says that were it not for a prior decree from God, a great punishment would have touched them for what they took. Verse 8:69 then says, 'So eat of what you have taken in spoils, lawful and good,' and the hadith says God made the spoils lawful for them. The aftermath was not only the kindness shown to the captives. It included this rebuke, and then the permission.
The courtyards of learning in Madinah where literacy and knowledge were fostered.

The return to Madinah was accompanied by both jubilation and bittersweet grief. Zayd ibn Harithah and Abdullah ibn Rawahah had galloped ahead on the Prophet's camels to announce the victory. Yet as the army entered the oasis, they learned that the Prophet's beloved daughter Ruqayyah had passed away from severe illness while her husband Uthman ibn Affan nursed her, having remained behind under prophetic instruction.

In Makkah, news of the catastrophe struck like an earthquake. The sole survivor of the vanguard, Al-Haysuman ibn Iyas, rode into the city in shock. When the chiefs asked for news, he stammered: 'By God, we met them and it was as though we offered our shoulders to them to slaughter us as they pleased! Utbah is slain, Shaybah is slain, Abu Jahl is slain!'

Makkah plunged into paralyzed disbelief. Abu Sufyan, who now assumed sole leadership of Quraysh, strictly forbade all public wailing or lamentation, so that the Muslims would not rejoice at their sorrow. He swore a solemn vow never to apply perfume or approach his wives until he launched an expedition of vengeance. The victory of Badr had redefined Arabia: the myth of Quraysh's invincibility was shattered, and the seeds of the next monumental clash were sown.
